note: Draft content. Correct choices are stewardship actions only: no diagnosis, no medicine choice, no doses. Needs review by a pharmacist and a veterinarian before publishing.

cases.title: The pharmacy counter
cases.intro: Your younger brother Tunde has had a runny nose and cough for two days. A neighbour says, “Just buy antibiotics, it will clear fast.” You walk to the pharmacy near your house.

steps.prompt: The attendant offers to sell you a strip of antibiotics without a prescription. What do you do?

choices.text: Buy them. The neighbour said it works.
choices.outcome: Antibiotics bought without advice may not be needed at all. Every unneeded use adds selection pressure, so resistant bacteria survive and spread.

choices.text: Ask to speak with the pharmacist about whether Tunde should be seen at a clinic.
choices.outcome: Good stewardship. A qualified pharmacist or health worker decides if any medicine is needed. You did not guess.

choices.text: Buy only half the strip to save money.
choices.outcome: Buying part of a pack without advice is still self-medication. It does not reduce the risk of resistance.

steps.prompt: Tunde rests, drinks fluids and feels better. At home you find old antibiotics left over from last year. What do you do with them?

choices.text: Keep them in the drawer for next time.
choices.outcome: Old leftovers tempt people to self-medicate later, and they may be expired or wrong for the next illness.

choices.text: Give them to Tunde now, just in case.
choices.outcome: Medicines should only be used when a health worker says they are needed. Using them “just in case” adds selection pressure.

choices.text: Take them back to the pharmacy and ask how to dispose of them safely.
choices.outcome: Right call. Safe disposal keeps leftovers out of homes, rivers and soil.

steps.prompt: Your family WhatsApp group is sharing a message that says “antibiotics cure every cough.” How do you respond?

choices.text: Say nothing. It is not your business.
choices.outcome: Myths spread fastest when nobody answers them. A short, kind reply can help.

choices.text: Reply that antibiotics do not work on viruses, and that a health worker should decide when they are needed.
choices.outcome: You shared an accurate message without diagnosing anyone. That is stewardship in action.

choices.text: Reply that people should buy the strongest antibiotic they can find.
choices.outcome: “Stronger” is not safer. Using medicines without need, whatever the type, drives resistance.

cases.summary: You avoided self-medication, cleared out leftovers safely and corrected a myth. All three protect antibiotics for when they are truly needed.

cases.title: The poultry farm
cases.intro: You are helping on your uncle’s poultry farm during the holidays. A few birds look weak and are eating less. A feed seller visits.

steps.prompt: The feed seller says: “Mix antibiotics into all the feed. The birds will grow faster and won’t fall sick.” What do you advise your uncle?

choices.text: Mix antibiotics into all the feed as the seller says.
choices.outcome: Using antimicrobials to make healthy animals grow faster is a major driver of resistance in farms.

choices.text: Call a veterinarian to examine the flock before any medicine is used.
choices.outcome: Correct. A vet decides if treatment is needed. The decision is not yours or the seller’s.

choices.text: Buy the cheapest medicine at the market and try it.
choices.outcome: Unknown medicines can be fake or wrong, and trying them without advice adds selection pressure.

steps.prompt: The vet says good biosecurity will stop infections spreading. Which plan do you follow?

choices.text: Let visitors and traders walk through the pens as usual.
choices.outcome: People, boots and crates carry microbes from farm to farm.

choices.text: Separate weak birds, clean and disinfect pens, use a footbath and limit visitors.
choices.outcome: Strong biosecurity prevents infections, so fewer medicines are needed.

choices.text: Throw dead birds into the stream behind the farm.
choices.outcome: This spreads microbes into water that people and animals use.

steps.prompt: The vet gives instructions for the sick birds, including a waiting time before eggs can be sold. A buyer wants eggs today. What do you do?

choices.text: Follow the vet’s instructions fully, including the waiting time before selling eggs.
choices.outcome: Correct. Waiting times keep medicine residues out of food.

choices.text: Sell the eggs today. The buyer will not know.
choices.outcome: Selling before the waiting time can put medicine residues into food.

choices.text: Stop the treatment early and keep the rest for next time.
choices.outcome: Changing the vet’s plan and storing leftovers leads to misuse later. Ask the vet before changing anything.

cases.summary: You brought in a vet, used biosecurity to prevent infection and respected the waiting time. That is One Health stewardship on a farm.
